q: The chapter "Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom" is an extract from whose autobiography?
o: Mahatma Gandhi
Nelson Mandela
Martin Luther King Jr.
Barack Obama
e: This lesson is an excerpt from the autobiography "Long Walk to Freedom" by Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela, South Africa's first Black President.

q: On which date did the historic inauguration of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government take place?
o: 15 August 1994
26 January 1994
2 October 1990
e: The chapter opens with "Tenth May dawned bright and clear"—the inauguration took place on 10 May 1994.

q: Where did the inauguration ceremonies take place?
o: In Cape Town Parliament
In Durban Main Stadium
In Johannesburg Town Hall
In the lovely sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria
e: The ceremonies took place in the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria, previously the seat of white supremacy.

q: Who accompanied Nelson Mandela on the day of the inauguration?
o: Indira
Winnie
Zenani
Anne
e: Mandela writes: "On that lovely autumn day I was accompanied by my daughter Zenani."

q: What was the political system that separated people according to their race in South Africa called?
o: Democracy
Apartheid
Socialism
Colonialism
e: "Apartheid" was the official political system of racial segregation and discrimination in South Africa.

q: According to Nelson Mandela, what is a country's greatest wealth?
o: Its people
The minerals and gems beneath its soil
Its military power
Its modern technology
e: Mandela declares that while South Africa is rich in minerals and gems, its greatest wealth is "its people, finer and truer than the purest diamonds."

q: What was the name of Nelson Mandela's party that won 252 of 400 seats in South Africa's first democratic elections?
o: United Democratic Party
South African Liberal Front
National Freedom League
African National Congress (ANC)
e: As noted in "Before You Read", Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) party won 252 of the 400 seats in the first democratic elections.

q: Who was sworn in as the First Deputy President before Nelson Mandela took the oath?
o: Mr de Klerk
Oliver Tambo
Thabo Mbeki
Walter Sisulu
e: Mr de Klerk was first sworn in as second deputy president, and then Thabo Mbeki was sworn in as first deputy president.

q: Who was sworn in as Second Deputy President during the inauguration?
o: Thabo Mbeki
Mr de Klerk
Bram Fischer
Robert Sobukwe
e: The text explicitly states: "On the podium, Mr de Klerk was first sworn in as second deputy president."

q: According to Mandela, how many obligations does every man have in life?
o: Two (twin obligations)
One
Three
Five
e: Mandela explains that "every man has twin obligations": obligations to his family and obligations to his people, community, and country.

q: What are the "twin obligations" described by Nelson Mandela?
o: To wealth and power
To his school and sports
To his friends and business
To his family and to his country/community
e: The twin obligations are (1) to one's family (parents, wife, children) and (2) to one's people, community, and country.

q: According to Nelson Mandela, what comes more naturally to the human heart?
o: Hate
Jealousy
Love
Fear
e: Mandela asserts that people must learn to hate, whereas "love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite."

q: Approximately how many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison before becoming South Africa's first Black President?
o: Ten years
Thirty years
Fifteen years
Forty years
e: According to the NCERT introductory note, Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first Black President "having spent thirty years in prison."

q: Politicians and dignitaries from more than how many countries attended Mandela's inauguration?
o: More than 140 countries
50 countries
80 countries
More than 200 countries
e: The NCERT introduction records that politicians and dignitaries from more than 140 countries around the world attended the ceremony.

q: What did Mandela learn about the true meaning of courage?
o: Complete absence of fear
Displaying physical strength
Fighting recklessly
Not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it
e: Mandela learned that "courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it"—the brave person is one who conquers fear.

q: Which colours of the new South African flag were left as a smoke trail by the chevron of Impala jets?
o: Saffron, white, green and blue
Red, white and purple
Black, red, green, blue and gold
Yellow, green and black only
e: The chevron of Impala jets left a smoke trail of the black, red, green, blue and gold of the new South African flag.

q: Which two national anthems were sung at the inauguration ceremony?
o: God Save the Queen and Vande Mataram
Nkosi Sikelel -iAfrika and Die Stem
La Marseillaise and Nkosi Sikelel
Die Stem and Jana Gana Mana
e: Two anthems were sung: the whites singing "Nkosi Sikelel -iAfrika" and the blacks singing "Die Stem", the old anthem of the Republic.

q: Who is the poet of "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Leslie Norris
Robert Frost
Walt Whitman
Carl Sandburg
e: The poem "A Tiger in the Zoo" was written by Leslie Norris.

q: Where is the tiger kept in the poem "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: In a dense forest
In a mountain cave
In a circus tent
Locked in a concrete cell / cage in a zoo
e: The tiger is "locked in a concrete cell, / His strength behind bars" inside a zoo, longing for the wild.

q: In "A Tiger in the Zoo", why should the tiger be lurking in shadow near the water hole?
o: To watch zoo visitors
To hide from patrolling cars
To catch plump deer passing by
To drink water and sleep
e: The tiger should be lurking in shadow near the water hole "Where plump deer pass" so it can hunt its natural prey.

q: What does the word "plump" mean in "Where plump deer pass"?
o: Thin
Fat / well-fed
Tiny
Weak and sick
e: "Plump" means pleasantly fat or well-fed, describing healthy deer in the wild.

q: What does "stalks" mean in "He stalks in his vivid stripes"?
o: Walks slowly and quietly/proudly in confined steps
Sleeps soundly
Roars loudly
Runs rapidly
e: In this context, "stalks" means paces or walks slowly with stiff, measured steps inside the cramped cage.

q: What is the last voice the tiger hears at night in the zoo?
o: Deer calling in the jungle
Chirping birds
Shouting villagers
The patrolling cars
e: The final stanza reads: "He hears the last voice at night, / The patrolling cars."

q: At what does the caged tiger stare with his brilliant eyes at night?
o: The zookeeper
Pieces of meat
The brilliant stars
The lock on his cage
e: He "stares with his brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars," symbolizing a silent yearning for freedom.

q: According to the third stanza of "A Tiger in the Zoo", how would the tiger terrorise the village in the wild?
o: By leaping from tall trees
Snarling around houses at the jungle's edge, baring his white fangs and claws
By swimming across rivers
By breaking iron bars
e: Stanza 3 depicts him "snarling around houses / At the jungle's edge, / Baring his white fangs, his claws, / Terrorising the village!"

q: According to Mandela, the structure of white racial domination was erected a few years after which bitter conflict?
o: Anglo-Boer war
First World War
American Civil War
Second World War
e: Mandela explicitly mentions it was erected "a few years after the bitter Anglo-Boer war and before my own birth."

q: Which season of the year in South Africa was 10 May, the inauguration day?
o: Spring
Monsoon
Summer
Autumn
e: In the Southern Hemisphere May falls in autumn, and Mandela directly calls it "that lovely autumn day".

q: In Mandela's speech, "We, who were outlaws not so long ago...", what does "outlaws" refer to?
o: Foreign tourists
Common bank robbers
South Africans and a nation cut off from international diplomatic relations due to apartheid
Prison wardens
e: Because of apartheid, many nations had severed diplomatic ties with South Africa and branded anti-apartheid leaders as outlaws.

q: How does the caged tiger react to the visitors in the zoo?
o: Charges and roars at them
Ignores them ("Ignoring visitors")
Begs them for food
Feels happy seeing them
e: Stanza 4 states: "Stalking the length of his cage, / Ignoring visitors," showing his helpless detachment and pride.

q: In Nelson Mandela's view, what is the oppressor a prisoner of?
o: Hatred, prejudice, and narrow-mindedness
A court of law
Poverty and starvation
Foreign armies
e: Mandela concludes: "A man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred; he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness."

q: Which of the following leaders is NOT among the six extraordinary South African patriots named by Mandela in the chapter?
o: Martin Luther King Jr. and Abraham Lincoln
Chief Luthuli and Yusuf Dadoo
Bram Fischer and Robert Sobukwe
Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu
e: Mandela explicitly names Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer, and Robert Sobukwe—not the American leaders Lincoln or King.

q: Why did Mandela reflect that "Perhaps it requires such depths of oppression to create such heights of character"?
o: Because white rulers built good schools
Because oppression strengthens national GDP
Because imprisonment is legally required to become President
Because extreme brutality of apartheid forged patriots of extraordinary courage, wisdom, and generosity
e: Mandela observed that decades of brutal apartheid unintendedly produced comrades of extraordinary courage, wisdom, and generosity.

q: As a young boy growing up in his village, what did Mandela think "freedom" meant?
o: The right to vote in elections
Staying out at night and reading what he pleased
Running in fields near his mother's hut, swimming in the clear stream, roasting mealies under the stars, and riding slow bulls
Earning his keep and marrying in Johannesburg
e: As a boy, Mandela felt free as long as he could run in the fields, swim in the clear stream, roast mealies under the stars, and ride slow-moving bulls.

q: Later as a student, which "transitory freedoms" did Mandela yearn for?
o: Swimming in streams and herding cattle
Staying out at night, reading what he pleased, and going where he chose
Becoming President of South Africa
Moving permanently abroad
e: As a student, he wanted the transitory freedoms of staying out at night, reading what he pleased, and going where he chose.

q: As a young man in Johannesburg, which "basic and honourable freedoms" did Mandela yearn for?
o: Achieving his potential, earning his keep, marrying, and having a family
Roasting mealies under the stars
Becoming an army general
Travelling freely around Europe
e: In Johannesburg he yearned for the basic, honourable freedoms of achieving his potential, earning his keep, marrying, and having a family.

q: When did Mandela's hunger for his own freedom become the greater hunger for the freedom of his people?
o: When he walked into the Pretoria amphitheatre
When he first joined primary school
When election results were announced on 10 May 1994
When he saw that not only he, but all his brothers and sisters who looked like him were not free
e: Realizing his boyhood freedom was an illusion and that everyone who looked like him was unfree, his personal desire transformed into a hunger for his people's freedom, leading him to join the ANC.

q: Why was Mandela "overwhelmed with a sense of history" on the day of the inauguration?
o: Because the Union Buildings were centuries old
Because he used to teach history
Because the harsh racial domination built in the 1900s was overturned forever in the final decade of that very century
Because he remembered his school days
e: He reflected on how the inhumane racial system built in the first decade of the 20th century was replaced in its last decade by a system recognizing equal rights for all.

q: What did the highest generals of the South African defence force and police do during the inauguration?
o: They boycotted the ceremony
They saluted Mandela and pledged their loyalty to him
They lit fireworks
They distributed copies of the new constitution
e: Bedecked with ribbons and medals, the highest generals saluted Mandela and pledged loyalty—though years earlier they would have arrested him.

q: Even in the grimmest times in prison, what kept Mandela going and assured him of human goodness?
o: A glimmer of humanity in one of the guards, perhaps just for a second
Poems printed in newspapers
Songs sung outside prison
News about South Africa's mines
e: Mandela recalls seeing "a glimmer of humanity in one of the guards, perhaps just for a second", proving man's goodness is a flame never extinguished.

q: What optimistic observation did Mandela make about the two national anthems sung on 10 May 1994?
o: One anthem would be banned the next day
Only school children would memorize them
Only the military band would perform them
Though neither group then knew the lyrics of the anthem they once despised, they would soon know the words by heart
e: Though neither group knew the words of the anthem they once despised, Mandela trusted they would soon know both by heart as one united nation.

q: When Mandela says "I was simply the sum of all those African patriots who had gone before me", what quality does this show?
o: Arrogance about personal fame
Fear of losing power
Humility and deep gratitude toward the countless martyrs before him
Jealousy toward earlier leaders
e: Mandela refuses personal credit, humbly seeing himself as the culmination of the unimaginable sacrifices of earlier African patriots.

q: Why was it impossible for a man of Mandela's birth and colour to fulfil both of his twin obligations in South Africa?
o: Because there were no courts in South Africa
Because attempting to serve his people meant being punished, isolated, and ripped away from his family
Because Black people could not speak to their mothers
Because schools banned history lessons
e: Trying to live as a human being and serve his people caused a Black man to be punished, isolated, and torn from his home and family.

q: According to Mandela, what transformed a frightened young man into a bold one and a law-abiding attorney into a criminal?
o: The intense hunger for the freedom of all his people and realizing the chains on any one were chains on all
Desire for wealth and fame
Military weapons training
Foreign funding
e: The desire for his people's dignity and freedom transformed a frightened young man into a bold rebel and a family-loving husband into a man without a home.

q: In his inauguration pledge, what forms of continuing bondage does Mandela vow to liberate all people from?
o: Foreign languages
Only taxation and tariffs
Mandatory military service
Poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender, and other discrimination
e: His exact words pledge liberation "from the continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination."

q: What is the central contrast highlighted across the stanzas of "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Speed of lions vs cheetahs
Daytime heat vs night cold
The helpless confinement of the tiger in a zoo cage versus its natural, majestic freedom in the jungle
Fear of children vs adults
e: The poem alternates between the cramped zoo cell (stanzas 1, 4, 5) and the tiger's natural wild habitat (stanzas 2, 3) to condemn captivity.

q: Why are the tiger's paws described as "pads of velvet quiet" in "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Because zookeepers put velvet shoes on him
Because his cushioned paws are soft like velvet and make no sound as he paces
Because the cage floor is carpeted with velvet
Because his paws are bandaged
e: A tiger's padded feet are soft like velvet, allowing the powerful predator to move silently without making a sound.

q: Why is the tiger described as being in "quiet rage" inside the cage?
o: He is furious at being imprisoned, yet helpless behind concrete walls and bars to unleash his fury
He is peaceful and content
He is suffering from fever
He is sleepy after a heavy meal
e: Though enraged by captivity, he realizes his strength is trapped behind bars, forcing him to suppress his anger silently.

q: According to Stanza 4 of "A Tiger in the Zoo", where is the tiger's strength locked?
o: Inside a village barn
Inside a wooden box
Across a deep valley
Behind bars in a concrete cell
e: The lines read: "But he's locked in a concrete cell, / His strength behind bars."

q: Which rhyme scheme is consistently followed in every stanza of "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: aabb
abab
abcb
abba
e: In each 4-line stanza, lines 2 and 4 rhyme (cage/rage, grass/pass, edge/village, bars/visitors, cars/stars), giving the abcb rhyme scheme.

q: In the final lines "And stares with his brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars", what does repeating the word "brilliant" suggest?
o: Bright floodlights installed in the zoo
A poignant connection between the tiger's fiery, unbroken spirit and the distant, free brilliance of the night sky
That the tiger is good at mathematics
That shooting stars are falling
e: Repeating "brilliant" links the undimmed wild spark in the tiger's eyes with the free, infinite night sky beyond his cage.

q: What does Mandela mean by "a twilight existence of secrecy and rebellion"?
o: Being forced under apartheid to live in hiding, secrecy, and rebellion instead of open normal family life
Playing outdoor games at dusk
Evening prayer rituals
Closing shops at sunset
e: Under apartheid, serving one's people meant being forced away from family into a shadowy underground life of secrecy and resistance.

q: Which statement from Mandela's chapter best highlights his unshakeable optimism about human nature?
o: "Chains are stronger than human courage."
"The sun will never rise on this land again."
"People are born hating each other forever."
"Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished."
e: Mandela's line "Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished" captures his enduring optimism even after prison.

q: How did ordinary South African citizens celebrate on the day of Mandela's inauguration?
o: Only foreign guests were permitted outside
Citizens stayed locked indoors in fear
More than 100,000 South African men, women, and children of all races sang and danced with joy
Crowds protested against the ANC
e: As stated in the text, over 100,000 South African men, women, and children of all races sang and danced together with joy.

q: Which stanzas of "A Tiger in the Zoo" describe the tiger's natural life in the jungle?
o: Stanzas 1 and 4
Stanzas 2 and 3
Stanzas 4 and 5
Stanza 1 only
e: Stanzas 2 (water hole and plump deer) and 3 (jungle's edge and village) depict the wild, while Stanzas 1, 4, and 5 show captivity.

q: How did Mandela describe the peaceful transfer of power in South Africa ("after centuries of white rule")?
o: A "rainbow gathering of different colours and nations"
A temporary truce
A military coup
An economic merger
e: Mandela called the diverse international and multiracial assembly a "rainbow gathering of different colours and nations".

q: In his speech "The sun shall never set on so glorious a human achievement", what does that achievement refer to?
o: Discovery of new diamond mines
Purchase of Impala fighter jets
Construction of the Union Buildings
The triumph of justice, peace, human dignity, and democratic freedom over apartheid
e: The "glorious human achievement" refers to the hard-won freedom and the victory for justice, peace, and human dignity.

q: What does the word "fangs" mean in "Baring his white fangs, his claws"?
o: Bright ears
Neck fur
Long sharp teeth
Tail bristles
e: "Fangs" are the long, sharp canine teeth of predatory animals like tigers.

q: When did Mandela realize that his boyhood freedom was actually "an illusion"?
o: When he visited the Union Buildings in 1994
As a young man, when he discovered his freedom had already been taken from him under apartheid
When he became Deputy President
When his daughter Zenani grew up
e: He realized his boyhood freedom was an illusion when, as a young man, he discovered his basic freedoms had already been denied by racial laws.

q: Which animal is mentioned passing near the water hole in "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Plump deer
Wild elephant
Tiny rabbit
Spotted leopard
e: The poem specifies "Near the water hole / Where plump deer pass."

q: What does "emancipation" mean in the context of Mandela's chapter ("the political emancipation we have achieved")?
o: Imposing new taxes
Expanding national borders
Cancelling elections
Freedom from legal, political, or social restriction
e: Per the NCERT glossary, "emancipation" means freedom from restriction or oppression.

q: Extract: "We thank all of our distinguished international guests for having come to take possession with the people of our country of what is, after all, a common victory for justice, for peace, for human dignity." Why does Mandela call it a "common victory"?
o: Because it referred to an international sports tournament
Because international guests voted in South Africa's elections
Because foreign armies conquered South Africa
Because ending apartheid was a shared moral triumph for universal values of justice, peace, and human dignity across all nations
e: World nations had stood against apartheid through sanctions and solidarity, making this triumph of human dignity a shared global victory.

q: In the line "all of our distinguished international guests", what does "distinguished" mean?
o: Ordinary and unknown
Angry and resentful
Respected, eminent, and honoured
Defeated and helpless
e: Here "distinguished" means respected, honoured, and eminent (referring to world leaders attending the ceremony).

q: What does Nelson Mandela refer to by the phrase "an extraordinary human disaster that lasted too long"?
o: A massive earthquake and tsunami
The long, brutal system of racial oppression under Apartheid
World War II
A prolonged drought and famine
e: Mandela uses "extraordinary human disaster" to describe the long-lasting inhumanity of apartheid and racial discrimination.

q: According to Mandela, what did the aerial display of South African jets over the Union Buildings symbolize?
o: Not only pinpoint precision, but the military's loyalty to democracy and the newly elected free government
Threatening neighbouring countries
A celebration of higher military budgets
Purely recreational entertainment
e: Mandela notes it was "not only a display of pinpoint precision and military force, but a demonstration of the military's loyalty to democracy."

q: When Mandela notes that the same generals who now saluted him "would not have saluted but arrested me" not so many years before, what is highlighted?
o: Failure of prison security
Incompetence of military generals
Mandela's personal grudge against officers
The dramatic historical transformation from an oppressive police state to a reconciled democracy
e: It starkly contrasts the past and present—yesterday's imprisoned outlaw is today's President saluted by the former regime's top generals.

q: "Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished." Identify the literary device used in this line.
o: Hyperbole
Pun
Metaphor
Onomatopoeia
e: Comparing man's goodness directly to "a flame" without using "like" or "as" is a classic Metaphor.

q: What deep moral truth is implied in Mandela's statement, "The oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity"?
o: Only oppressors deserve liberation
Both suffer moral loss: the oppressed loses freedom, while the oppressor becomes a prisoner of hatred and prejudice, losing compassion
The oppressed are equally guilty of cruelty
Oppression makes rulers more compassionate
e: A person who steals another's freedom traps himself behind "bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness", meaning both need liberation to restore full humanity.

q: Why does Mandela say the desire for his people's freedom "drove a law-abiding attorney to become a criminal"?
o: Because under unjust apartheid laws, fighting peacefully for basic human dignity and equal rights was branded a crime
Because Mandela robbed banks to fund elections
Because he hated all forms of constitutional law
Because he committed tax fraud
e: When the legal system itself enforces racial oppression, demanding freedom and dignity inevitably turns a peaceful, law-abiding lawyer into an "outlaw" in the regime's eyes.

q: What does the word "curtailed" mean in the context of freedom being denied?
o: Expanded greatly
Made permanent
Publicly honoured
Reduced or restricted
e: "Curtailed" means cut short, reduced, or restricted.

q: In "The structure they created formed the basis of one of the harshest, most inhumane, societies...", who does "they" refer to?
o: Impala fighter pilots
Neighbouring African nations
The white-skinned peoples of South Africa who patched up their differences after the Anglo-Boer war
Indigenous tribal elders
e: "They" refers to the white-skinned peoples of South Africa who united after the Anglo-Boer war to erect a system of racial domination.

q: According to Mandela, what defines a "civil and humane society" regarding twin obligations?
o: A society where citizens have no duties
A society where every man is able to fulfil both obligations (to family and country) according to his own inclinations and abilities
A society ruled solely by military generals
A society that separates families permanently
e: Mandela explicitly says: "In a civil and humane society, each man is able to fulfil those obligations according to his own inclinations and abilities."

q: Identify the poetic device in the phrase "quiet rage" from "A Tiger in the Zoo".
o: Oxymoron
Simile
Hyperbole
Pun
e: "Quiet" (silent, calm) and "rage" (violent anger) are contradictory terms placed side by side, creating an Oxymoron.

q: Which poetic device is used in "On pads of velvet quiet" in "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Irony
Simile
Anaphora
Metaphor
e: The tiger's soft paws are directly equated to velvet without using "like" or "as", which is a Metaphor.

q: Throughout "A Tiger in the Zoo", the poet refers to the tiger as "He" instead of "it" and describes him "Ignoring visitors". Which device is this?
o: Onomatopoeia
Oxymoron
Personification
Pun
e: Calling the tiger "He" and attributing human emotions like quiet rage and deliberately ignoring visitors is Personification.

q: In "He should be snarling around houses / At the jungle's edge", the word "snarling" (an angry growling sound) illustrates which sound device?
o: Simile
Onomatopoeia
Anaphora
Oxymoron
e: "Snarling" imitates the fierce growling sound a tiger makes, making it an example of Onomatopoeia.

q: Identify the repeated consonant sounds showing Alliteration in "He stalks in his vivid stripes" and "His strength behind bars".
o: /s/ ("stalks... stripes") and /b/ ("behind bars")
/k/ and /p/
/m/ and /n/
/r/ and /t/
e: "stalks... stripes" repeats /s/ and "behind bars" repeats /b/ (just as "plump... pass" repeats /p/ and "he hears" repeats /h/).

q: In "Sliding through long grass / Near the water hole / Where plump deer pass", the continuation of a clause across lines without end punctuation is called:
o: Hyperbole
Oxymoron
Pun
Enjambment
e: Flowing seamlessly across line breaks without punctuation is Enjambment, mimicking the smooth sliding motion of the tiger through long grass.

q: What does the adjective "vivid" mean in "He stalks in his vivid stripes"?
o: Faded and dim
Short and broken
Bright, clear, and distinct
Purely white
e: "Vivid" means intensely bright, clear, and distinct—contrasting the tiger's majestic appearance with his cramped prison.

q: What does the imagery of a "concrete cell" emphasize in Stanza 4 of "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: A comfortable luxury palace
Cold, artificial, unyielding human-made imprisonment starkly opposite to soft jungle grass
A natural cave habitat
Industrial growth
e: The word "cell" evokes a human prison—cold, rigid, and unnatural compared to the living forest grass and water hole.

q: What can be inferred from the phrase "The few steps of his cage" in Stanza 1?
o: The cage is painfully cramped and tiny for a majestic wild beast built to roam miles of forest
The tiger is afraid to walk fast
There are only two tigers in the zoo
The tiger gets tired after three steps
e: "The few steps" highlights severe spatial confinement for an animal naturally meant to patrol vast jungle territories.

q: In Mandela's closing benediction "Let freedom reign. God bless Africa!", what does "reign" convey?
o: Rainfall during autumn
Limiting voting rights
Return of colonial monarchs
That freedom should prevail as the supreme, enduring rule across the nation
e: "Reign" means to rule or prevail supremely—wishing that liberty, not racial tyranny, will rule South Africa forever.

q: In "For weeks before the inauguration, I was pleasantly besieged by dignitaries and world leaders", what does "besieged" mean?
o: Attacked by enemy forces
Completely ignored
Surrounded closely (here, warmly crowded by admiring guests)
Hidden in isolation
e: According to NCERT glossary, "to be besieged by" means to be surrounded closely by—here pleasantly surrounded by paying-respect world dignitaries.

q: Which actions in "A Tiger in the Zoo" portray the tiger as fierce and natural when imagined in the wild?
o: Sleeping peacefully and ignoring tourists
Lurking in shadow, sliding through long grass, snarling around houses, and baring fangs and claws
Watching patrolling cars
Stalking a few steps in concrete
e: Active verbs in Stanzas 2–3 (lurking, sliding, snarling, baring, terrorising) vividly capture the tiger's natural power and instincts.

q: What does Mandela say about the "deep and lasting wound" created by apartheid in his country and people?
o: All South Africans will spend many years, if not generations, recovering from that profound hurt—though it also forged heroic character
It healed within one week after 10 May
It damaged only gold mines
It affected only foreign visitors
e: Mandela writes that apartheid left "a deep and lasting wound in my country and my people" requiring many years, if not generations, to heal.

q: What does "inclinations" mean in "according to his own inclinations and abilities"?
o: Financial debts
Strict prison rules
Mountain slopes
Natural tendencies or preferences of behaviour
e: The NCERT glossary defines "inclinations" as natural tendencies of behaviour.

q: What attitude of the tiger is revealed by the phrase "Ignoring visitors" in Stanza 4?
o: Expectation of treats
Affection for visitors
Helplessness combined with proud detachment—he refuses to entertain humans gawking at his captivity
Timidity and fear of children
e: Recognizing his strength is caged and visitors treat him as spectacle, he keeps his pride by coldly ignoring them.

q: What literary effect is created by pairing "depths of oppression" with "heights of character" in Mandela's reflection?
o: Comedic relief
Antithesis/Contrast showing how extreme suffering paradoxically gave rise to supreme moral greatness
Literal geographical measurement
Careless repetition
e: Contrasting "depths" with "heights" (Antithesis) emphasizes the paradox that extreme oppression cultivated extraordinary heroism.

q: What is the figurative implication of "His strength behind bars" in "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: The tiger's immense natural power and purpose are rendered useless and trapped behind artificial iron bars
The bars are weak and broken
The tiger exercises using iron rods

That zookeepers race cars for fun
e: Instead of rustling leaves and night forest calls, the tiger's day ends with mechanized surveillance, reinforcing how completely human control surrounds him.

q: Which statement best captures Mandela's philosophy of reconciliation after spending decades in prison?
o: Replacing racial vengeance with reconciliation so both oppressed and oppressor can rebuild a dignified, non-racial democracy
Expelling all white citizens from South Africa
Focusing exclusively on diamond mining
Erasing history books
e: Mandela rejected revenge, envisioning a non-racial society proud of justice and peace where both oppressed and oppressor reclaim their humanity.

q:
Arrange the following historical/biographical stages from "Long Walk to Freedom" in chronological order:
1. Creation of apartheid structure after the Anglo-Boer war
2. Mandela yearning for basic honourable freedoms in Johannesburg
3. Inauguration ceremony in Pretoria on 10 May 1994
4. Joining the ANC for collective freedom and enduring decades of prison
e: Order: Apartheid erected before Mandela's birth (1) → Young manhood in Johannesburg (2) → Joining ANC for his people's freedom and imprisonment (4) → 10 May 1994 inauguration (3).

q: What ethical question about zoos and wildlife does Leslie Norris subtly raise through "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Are zoo entry tickets overpriced?
Should tigers be kept as household pets in villages?
Does humanity have the moral right to rob wild creatures of their natural habitat and majesty merely for human amusement and display?
Should tigers be fed at midnight?
e: Portraying the zoo as a "concrete cell" where natural power withers challenges the ethics of confining wild animals for human entertainment.

q: Who does Mandela mean by "them" when he writes, "I was pained that I was not able to thank them and that they were not able to see what their sacrifices had wrought"?
o: Foreign journalists arriving late
The countless African patriots and comrades who died before seeing the triumph of freedom their sacrifices achieved
Retired prison wardens
Impala fighter pilots flying overhead
e: Amid celebration, Mandela mourned the thousands of patriots who gave their lives for liberation yet passed away before witnessing 10 May 1994.

q: Based strictly on the poem's imagery, which inner thought best matches the caged tiger's condition?
o: "My vivid stripes and fierce spirit belong to tall grass and starlit jungles; these few concrete steps mock my caged strength."
"I feel proud and safe inside this concrete cell because visitors admire me."
"I prefer concrete walls over lurking in shadows near water holes."
"The sound of patrolling cars soothes me into peaceful sleep."
e: His "quiet rage", "ignoring visitors", and staring at "brilliant stars" all prove his wild identity fiercely resents the cramped concrete cage.

q: What forced Mandela, originally a family-loving man, "to live like a monk" and become a man without a home?
o: Failure in his legal career
A dispute over family property
Desire to join a monastery
The overwhelming duty to fight for his people's freedom forced him to sacrifice normal domestic comfort and family life
e: Apartheid made fulfilling both obligations impossible; choosing to serve his oppressed people forced him to surrender domestic home life like a monk.

q: Which pair correctly identifies a Visual image and an Auditory image from "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: Visual: "quiet rage"; Auditory: "white fangs"
Visual: "last voice"; Auditory: "vivid stripes"
Visual: "vivid stripes" / "brilliant stars"; Auditory: "snarling around houses" / "patrolling cars"
Visual: "silent pads"; Auditory: "plump deer"
e: "Vivid stripes" and "brilliant stars" appeal to sight (visual), while "snarling" and hearing "the patrolling cars" appeal to sound (auditory).

q: Why does Mandela pledge liberation from "poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination" immediately after winning political freedom?
o: Because racial oppression had never existed
Because political freedom alone is incomplete without social, economic, and gender equality for every citizen
To request foreign loans immediately
To avoid discussing the new constitution
e: Mandela recognized that true emancipation goes beyond ending political apartheid—it demands ending poverty, deprivation, and gender inequality too.

q: Which alternative title would best preserve the central theme of Leslie Norris's poem "A Tiger in the Zoo"?
o: "Caged Majesty: Freedom vs Confinement"
"The Dangerous Village Attack"
"A Fun Trip to the Zoo"
"Exercise on Velvet Paws"
e: The heart of the poem is the tragic tension between the tiger's natural majesty/freedom and unnatural concrete confinement.

q: In the title "Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom", what does the metaphor "Long Walk" signify?
o: The length of the amphitheatre steps
The literal walking distance from Pretoria to Johannesburg
Mandela's childhood strolls near the stream
That freedom was not won overnight, but through decades of relentless struggle, prison, suffering, patience, and collective sacrifice
e: "Long Walk" symbolizes the arduous, decades-long journey of sacrifice, imprisonment, resilience, and moral courage required to attain liberty.

q: According to Mandela, what inner quality sustained him and his comrades even when pushed to the limits of human endurance in prison?
o: Burning hatred toward guards
A secret tunnel to escape Robben Island
Unshakeable faith in human goodness ("a flame never extinguished") and selfless courage in overcoming fear
Hopes of winning international prizes
e: Belief in man's inextinguishable goodness, glimpsed even in a prison guard, along with courage that triumphs over fear kept him unbroken.

q: Trace the emotional arc from the opening line ("He stalks in his vivid stripes") to the closing line ("At the brilliant stars") in "A Tiger in the Zoo".
o: It moves from terror to joyous dancing
It moves from suppressed physical frustration ("quiet rage") through memories of wild power to silent, poignant longing toward the stars
It moves from hunger to a pleasant feast
It shows him sleeping peacefully throughout
e: The poem progresses from caged physical anger through imagined wild vitality to silent, wistful yearning beneath the distant stars.

q: Which detail from the inauguration day best illustrates Mandela's belief that "a country's greatest wealth is its people"?
o: Over 100,000 South Africans of all races singing and dancing together in joy, alongside the legacy of selfless patriots who built that day
The sandstone pillars of the Union Buildings
The fuel burned by Impala fighter jets
Expensive souvenirs given to diplomats
e: The joyful unity of 100,000+ citizens of all races and the heroic legacy of patriots prove that ordinary and extraordinary people are the nation's true diamonds.
